Khondoker Shahriar Shakir, with Suraya Jannat Sumy, Advocates—For the Plaintiff (Petitioner.).

Rony Anthony Rozario ------ Plaintiff (Petitioner)

full_judgment:
The plaintiff filed the instant Divorce Suit under section 18 of. the Divorce Act, 1869 for a decree declaring the marriage, between the Plaintiff and the Defendant bearing registration No.48/09, solemnized in the St. Nicholas Church, Nagari, Gazipur, before the Rev. Maxwell A Thomas, is null and void and for specifying the child in the decree who was begotten before the decree is made, to be entitled to succeed, in the same manner as legitimate children, to the estate of the parent who at the time of the marriage was competent to contract. 

 2. The plaintiff's case in short is that she and the Defendant both profess the Christian religion and got married on 25-9-2009 having solemnized in St Nicholas Church, Nagari bearing Registration No. 48/09, before Rev. Maxwell A Thomas and the Plaintiff and Defendant started their conjugal life as husband and wife at Village Karan in Gazipur—District. On the very first night of the marriage the Plaintiff recognized some abnormality in the behaviour of the Defendant as seemed to be in a conversation with someone invisible which the Plaintiff ignored at that time. After few months the Defendant started to create unrest situation with the parents of the Plaintiff and she insisted that she would not live with her old parents-in-law. The Plaintiff tried to console her as he was the only earning son of his parents and he wanted to live with them but the Defendant did not pay heed to his proposal and kept on quarreling with the family members of the Plaintiff. The Defendant threatened the Plaintiff that she would commit suicide if he does not arrange a separate living accommodation for her in Dhaka City. The Plaintiff continued to make her understand that he requires to live with them. Then the Defendant attempted to commit suicide by strangling on 18-1-2010 herself and some occasions thereof. Then an arbitration was held at instance of the Chairman of the local Union Parishad assisted by the people at locality but she misbehaved and disrespected them. In the meantime, the Defendant became pregnant and then she became furious and started damaging and breaking utensils and furniture. The defendant again threatened the Plaintiff that if he did not leave his ancestral house, she would take poison. During pregnancy, the Defendant again attempted to commit suicide by taking poison on 06-6-2010. The Plaintiff and his family members took her to the hospital and her stomach was washed which caused a threat to the life of the fetus in her womb. After that incidence the parents of the Defendant took her to her to their house and she trave birth a male child on 23-8-2010. She returned to Plaintiff's house after the childbirth. She remained calm and quiet for few days and again she became restive and demanded to go to Dhaka city and live with son. The Plaintiff tried to resist her as she would not be able to maintain the child herself. The Plaintiff used to work in restaurant in Dhaka City in 2012. The Defendant suddenly came to Dhaka at the residence of the Plaintiff With son without informing the Plaintiff. The Plaintiff's attempt to return her at village Karan, Gazipur failed. Then the Plaintiff hired a small house to reside with her in Dhaka. She claimed for a big house so that her parents and younger brother can live with them. But the Plaintiff refused that proposal. Few days later the parents of the defendant came to their small house and started living there. The Defendant prohibited the plaintiff to contact to his parents and not to help them finanCially. The Plaintiff continued to help his parents financially and to look after them as they were ailing old persons. The Defendant made it an issue and continued quarreling and yelling to the Plaintiff. She threatened that she would cut off the throat of the Plaintiff and, she also threatened that she would commit suicide keeping a suicidal note so that the Plaintiff and his family might be in trouble. The Defendant left the house several times after quarreling with the Plaintiff and returned again. The Defendant sworn an affidavit, declaring the Divorce with the Plaintiff, on 04-4-2013, before a Notary Public, Mr Md Lukman Hussain, Advocate, Dhaka. Wherein she declared that she had relinquished the Plaintiff as her husband following the provisions of Christian Canon Law. The Plaintiff was at the veree of a break down with the conduct and behaviour of the Defendant. He took her to a psychiatrist, on 05-3-2017 and She was diagnosed with different types of mental health disorder, namely paranoia and delusion as well as suicidal and homicidal tendency and was advised to hospitalize her. The Defendant filed several false criminal cases against the Plaintiff to harass him and to make him suffer to the least. She filed a false case against the Plaintiff Nari-o-Shishu Petition Case No. 03/2021, on 13-1-2021, under section 11(Ga) of Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain. 2000 (As amended in 2020) before the Nari-o-Shishu Nidatan Daman Tribunal No.6, Dhaka. He was arrested on 14-3-2021 and was released on bail, vide Order No.5, dated 15-4-2021. The case is pending before the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal No.6, Dhaka. The Defendant filed another false criminal case against the Plaintiff and few other persons, bearing CR Case No, 58/ 2021, on 15-2-2021, before the Court of Senior Judicial Magistrate, Gazipur under sections 420, 406, 471 and 34 of Bangladesh Penal Code. The case was sent to PBI, Gazipur District for investigation. Sub-Inspector Mizanur Rahman investigated into the case and filed a report on 18-7-2021. In his investigation report the Investigation officer opined that there was no specific evidence to proof the crime under sections 420, 406. 471 and 34 of the Penal Code. Plaintiff and the Defendant had been living in a house at 58/2 Free School Street, Kathalbagan, Dhaka since May 2017. That time the unrestive behaviour of the Defendant got severe and she was continuously quarrelling and yelling with the Plaintiff using abusive words. She rushed with a Boti to chop off the Plaintiff on 20-5-2017 and the Plaintiff saved himself by fleeing from his house but she was shouting from the back that she would cut his throat when he would sleep. The Plaintiff made a general diary, bearing GD No. 879, dated 20-5-2017, in Kalabagan Police Station informing the incident. The defendant was diagnosed with paranoia and delusion of infel. Her suicidal and homicidal tendency was mentioned by the psychiatrist and she was advised to hospitalize. The Plaintiff realized about her insanity from the first day of their marital life. The Defendant had a prolonged history of disturbed mental health since before marriage. She was a lunatic at the time of the marriage. The Plaintiff prayed for a decree declaring the marriage between the Plaintiff and the Defendant to be null and void. Besides to specify the child in the decree who was born before the decree to be made as to be entitled to succeed, in the same manner as legitimate children to the estate of the parent who at the time of the marriage was competent to contract, following the provisions of section 21 of the Divorce Act, 1869. 

 1) Whether the suit is maintainable in the present form under the Divorce Act, 1869 of Bangladesh: 

 8) The Plaintiff by filing another application under section 7 of the Divorce Act, 1869 prayed for an order dissolving the marriage, between the Plaintiff and the Defendant, considering the principles as stipulated in section 1(3) of the Matrimonial Causes Act, 1973 (1973 c 18), as amended by the Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act. 2020 of UK The defendant filed a written objection against the said application. 

 5. Mr. Khondoker Shahriar Shakir assisted by Ms. Suraya Jannat Sumy, learned advocate appearing for the plaintiff submits that the Divorce Act, 1869 along with its whole contents including section 7 was adapted by Bangladesh through the Bangladesh (Adaptation of Existing Laws) Order. 1972; President's Order No.48 of 1972. Section 7 of the Divorce Act. 1869 was neither repealed nor altered, nor amended by the Legislature or any other competent authority. Sections 2 and 3 of the President's Order No.48 of 1972 provides that— 

 6. Thus, the section 7 of the Divorce Act, 1869 is fully in operation under Bangladeshi legislation. The provisions laid therein is totally relevant and required to meet the needs of present time and it is mandatory to follow where required. 

 11. Learned counsel argued that since the Plaintiff deposed that the Defendant used to threaten the Plaintiff that she would cut his throat when he would sleep. Furthermore the Defendant chased him with a sharpened boti yelling that she would cut him off the Plaintiff tied away from home and made a general diary, bearing No 829, dated 20-5-2017 in Kalabagan Police Station. Besides, she used to commit domestic abuse, verbal abuse, shouting and belittling the Plaintiff as her usual nature. The Defendant also attempted to commit suicide several times. Furthermore, the Plaintiff and the Defendant has been living separately since November 2020, as deposed by the Defendant in cross-examination. Such separation is to be regarded as Separation with Consent. The Defendant did not file any case for restitution of conjugal life under section 32 of the Act, even after separation of more that 3 (three) years, as such she is not willing to continue with this marriage. It is evident from the documentary and oral evidences that the Defendant sworn an affidavit declaring divorce with the Plaintiff on 04-4-2013, before the Notary Public. The Defendant filed 2 (two) criminal cases against the Plaintiff One is Nari-o-Sishu Petition Case No.03 of 2021, dated 13-1-2021 under section 11Ga under Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 2000, filed before the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal No.6, Dhaka and the another is CR Case No.58 of 2021, dated 15-2-2021, filed before the Senior Judicial Magistrate Gazipur. Out of which CR Case No. 58 of 2021 is dismissed and the Nari-o-Sishu Petition Case No.03 of 2021 is pending but the Defendant does not appear in the case, knowing that the case has no merit and it will be dismissed as well. The Defendant caused the Plaintiff arrested in the Nari-o-Sishu Petition Case No.03 of 2021 and the Plaintiff was in custody for one month for a false allegation. Thus, since it is claimed by the Plaintiff and by the act of the Defendant it has been proved that the marriage has broken down irretrievably. The Plaintiff is entitled to get an order from this court to dissolve this marriage following the provisions of section 7 of the Divorce Act, 1869. 

 12. Per contra, Mr. Kawser Ahmed. learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party submits "a marriaee broken down irretrievably" is not a around for declaring a marriage null and void under section 19 of the Divorce Act, 1869 and thus, it is hit by "Subject to the provisions contained in this Act" of the section 18 of the same Act. 

 13. He again submits that recognising "a marriage broken down irretrievably" as a ground for declaring a marriage null and void under section 19 of the Divorce Act, 1869 will amount to assumption of legislative power by the court and thus, it goes against the decision of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in Nishat Jute Mills Limited vs Human Rights and Peace for Bangladesh (HRPB), Appellate Division, CPLA No. 3039 of 2019, Judgment delivered on 17 February 2020, at 35-37. 

 14. Mr. Kawser Ahmed further submits that claiming a marriage null and void on the grounds that "a marriage broken down irretrievably" is entirely contrary to the pleadings of the Plaintiff that the defendant was an "Idiot" or "Lunatic" at the time of the marriage and thus, the marriage was a nullity. A Plaintiff can pray for a declaration of marriage as null and void on the grounds of "Idiocy" or "Lunacy" under section 19 of the Divorce Act, 1869. However, such a decree cannot be granted for other reasons like "irretrievable breaking-down of marriage" 

 15. He further submits that the plaintiff sought relief as per UK Statutes e.g., the Matrimonial Causes Act, 1973 and the Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020 under section 7 of the Divorce Act, 1869 ignoring that section 7 of the said Act does not approve of direct incorporation of UK Statutes blindly which is inimical to the sovereignty of Bangladesh. 

 16. He also cited two reported cases, i.e. Mrs. Marie Antoinette vs Oaivald Robert Palmer 1(1957) 9 DLR (WP Lahore) 251, where the Lahore High Court relied upon section 7 of the Divorce Act. 1869 to award litigation cost to the Plaintiff for the reason that there was no such provision in the said Act (para. 78. at pp. 26-27). In Farooci teivers vs Adelaide Bridget May 1(1958) 10 DLR (WP Lahore) 591, the Lahore High Court invoked section 7 to rely on a decision of the King's Bench to find a solution in a scenario of conflict of personal law situation between the parties (para. 22-23. at pp. 67-68) According to him, there are no reported cases during 1948-2023 wherein marriage between Christians were held null and void on the grounds of "Idiocy" or "Lunacy". However, in these two reported cases section 7 was invoked by the court, but there was no precedent of application of section 7 by the Court purporting to broaden the scope of the grounds for declaring a marriage null and void under section 19 of the Divorce Act, 1869. 

 19. The concept of mental disorder is far beyond the concept of lunacy in its nature, proces of identification and in terms related to human dignity. And the concept of +Lunacy has been rescinded with the repeal of the Lunacy Act, 1912 by the Manoshik Shastho Ain, 2018. As the term lunacy contends of humiliation and lack of human dignity the modern legislative trend is to replace the term lunacy with the mental disorder. As such, as the status of a lunatic is no more appreciated by the existing laws of Bangladesh a remedy under section 19(3) of the Divorce Act, 1869 cannot be provided at its grammatical contention. 

 20. It also can be noted that before enactment of the Divorce Act. 1869, in the UK the enactment of the divorce act took place in 1857 in the name of the Matrimonial Causes Act, 1857, for the first time. Under that law reasons for divorce were considered as— 

 21. In course of time, the law related to divorce in the UK was amended time to time. After the enactment of Matrimonial Causes Act, 1857, the law was further amended in the same year and the concept of adultery and incurable insanity was inserted as the causes of divorce. Wherefrom, the Lunacy was regarded as a cause for divorce under the Divorce Act, 1869, enacted during British colonial regime. 

 23. Here it may be noted that although the enactment during 1857 in UK contended lunacy as a ground for divorce, lunacy or incurable insanity has been intrigued with the concept of unreasonable behavior, as a reason for divorce, in course of time and that continued until the enactment of 2022. Unreasonable behavior was a more expanded cause of divorce which included cruelty and insanity. But in Bangladesh, following the legacies of British-Indian regime, Pakistan regime the causes of divorce remain the same as 1869, as no amendment took place in law in this regard. 

 24. Under Bangladeshi Legal arena the Divorce Act, 1869 has been adapted by sections 2 and 3 of the President's Order No.48 of 1972 and the Act is still existing without any repeal, alteration or amendment by the legislature and the competent authority. The whole of the Divorce Act, 1869 including section 7 of the Act stands as a law of Bangladesh by virtue of sections 2 and 3 of the President's Order No.48 of 1972. 

 25. Although the laws related to divorce has not been amended since 1869 in Bangladesh, there is a window remains in the closed walls of the century old private law to welcome the flow of the fresh air of present legal understandings, thoughts and theories by section 7 of the Divorce Act, 1869 whereby the Court is to act on principles and rules as followed by the English Divarce Court, for the time being, while trying a case under this Act. Section 7 of the Divorce Suit 1869 provides that- 

 32. Furthermore, the plaintiff prayed for an order dissolving the marriage by filing an application under section 7 of the Divorce Act. The section allows to consider the standard of principles and rules followed by the English Court of the time being while determining matters under the Divorce Act, 1869. There is no possibility of being inimical to the sovereignty of Bangladesh by passing such order, as submitted by Mr Kawser Ahmed. learned Counsel of the defendant. Because the Divorce Act, 1869 is adapted in Bangladeshi legal regime by sections 2 and 3 of the Bangladesh (Adaptation of Existing Laws) Order. 1972. President's Order No. 48 of 1972. 

 33. Mr. Kawser Ahmed argued that "a marriage broken down irretrievably as a ground for declaring a marriage null and void under section 19 of the Divorce Act, 1869 will amount to assumption of legislative power by the court and thus, it goes against the decision of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in Nishat Jute Mills Limited vs. Human Rights and Peace for Bangladesh (HRPB), reported in ALR 23 (AD) 39 and 17 ADC 401. Paragraphs 35-37 are not relevant to this case. Rather paragraph 39 provides a fare guideline for the High Court Division for determining the adaptation of laws those are not enacted by the Parliament. Paragraph 39 provides that. 

 35. In the present case The Divorce Act, 1869 along with its section 7 has been adapted by the appropriate legislative authority of Bangladesh vide Presidential Order No. 42 of 1972. There is no confusion that section 7 of this Act is applicable with the approval of the appropriate legislative authority. According to this section of the Act there is no harm to consider the principles and rules followed by the English Courts in determining this divorce suit. 

 42. It may be further noted that in Anowar Hossain Chowdhury vs Government of Bangladesh and others, as reported in 41 DLR (AD) 165, the Appellate Division reminded in the ratio of the judgment, in paragraph No.623, that "The words "subject matter" must be given the widest meaning to include not only "cause of action" but also party, property, right, obligation, violation, etc. in connection with the matter so that a citizen is not refused before any bench on a technicality regard being always had to the fact that it is the same court". Bearing the principle in mind we are of the opinion that filing the suit under section 19(3) of the Divorce Act, 1869 does not debar this court to give relief to a party considering all aspects discussed above.
